960.title: Vincent of Saragossa (22 January)
960.hook: a deacon-martyr of Spain who spoke for his bishop, honored by vine-growers
960.tomorrow: Francis de Sales, patron of writers (24 January)
960.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Vincent's day in January, and in some wine regions growers mark it with a Mass and a blessing of the vines.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sebastian: the soldier who survived the arrows and went back to face the emperor. Your line was arrows didn't stop him. What knocked you flat, and who helped you up? Day nine hundred sixty.

Two prisoners stand in front of a Roman governor in Spain. One is old, a bishop, Valerius of Saragossa. The other is young, his deacon, Vincent. The governor asks his questions, and the bishop, the story says, struggles to get the words out. So the deacon turns to him and asks permission to answer for them both. Then Vincent speaks, clearly and without fear, and the governor's patience snaps. The bishop is sent into exile. The deacon is kept back for something worse. Today, a new week of the calendar, and a deacon who lent his voice.
screen: `A BISHOP AND HIS DEACON, ON TRIAL.` → `THE BISHOP STRUGGLES TO SPEAK.` → `THE DEACON ANSWERS FOR BOTH.`

segments.voice: Vincent's story comes to us through the early Church in poems and sermons. The Christian poet Prudentius wrote a long hymn to him, and Augustine of Hippo preached on his feast. Begin with what he was: a deacon. Behind the word deacon is the Greek diakonos, a servant, someone who waits on others. In the Acts of the Apostles, the apostles choose seven men to serve the community's tables so that widows aren't forgotten. Catholics see there the root of the job. Deacons serve the poor, read the Gospel at Mass, preach, and assist the bishop. Vincent served his bishop in a very literal way, by being his voice. After the trial, the story is grim. Vincent was tortured, stretched and burned, and thrown into a cell on broken pottery. And there, Prudentius sings, the dark cell filled with light, and the shards turned soft as flowers, and the jailer was converted. Vincent died of his wounds. The Church remembers him as a deacon-martyr of Spain. Then the vines. In wine country, vine-growers took Vincent as their patron. People give different reasons, and some are half a joke about his name. Whatever the reason, his day falls in the dead of winter, when the vines are bare and pruning begins, and in some villages growers still walk out to bless the vines in his name. Some readers hear his feast in a vineyard line from John's Gospel. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the vine: you the branches". In the same chapter, the branches that bear fruit are pruned, so they bear more. Winter work, on Vincent's day.
screen: `DIAKONOS: ONE WHO SERVES.` · `HE SPOKE FOR HIS BISHOP.` · `A DARK CELL FILLS WITH LIGHT.` · `WINTER VINES, BLESSED IN HIS NAME.` · then, large: `I AM THE VINE: YOU THE BRANCHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless a vine or a plant. Settle, and breathe. Find a living plant near you, a houseplant, a tree outside the window, herbs on a sill. If there isn't one, bring one to mind. Look at it closely: the stems, the new growth, the dead leaves. Pick one dead leaf off, gently, the way a vine-grower prunes in winter. If you pray, you can make the sign of the cross over it and ask God's blessing on it. If you don't, give it water and a moment of your attention. The bell holds the time.
Vincent of Saragossa. A deacon who spoke for his bishop at trial, died a martyr, and is honored by vine-growers in the middle of winter.
Your line: a deacon of spain. Today, be someone's voice once: speak up for a person who struggles to get the words out. Day nine hundred sixty.

961.title: Francis de Sales, patron of writers (24 January)
961.hook: when no one came to hear him, he slid pamphlets under doors
961.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Francis de Sales's memorial in January; writers and journalists honor him as their patron, and his Introduction to the Devout Life is still read by lay Catholics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vincent of Saragossa, the deacon who answered for his bishop. Your line was a deacon of spain. Whose voice were you, even for a sentence? Day nine hundred sixty-one.

A young priest stands in a village square in the hills south of Lake Geneva, ready to preach. Nobody comes. The town has become Reformed, Calvinist, and a Catholic preacher is not someone they want to hear. Doors stay shut. Some people won't even look at him in the street. He could leave. He could shout louder. Instead he goes home, sits down at a table, and starts to write. Short pages, clear and calm, one argument at a time. Then, the story goes, he walks through the town at night and slides them under the doors. Today, the man the Church calls a patron of writers.
screen: `A PREACHER, AND NOBODY COMES.` → `HE SITS DOWN AND WRITES.` → `PAGES UNDER THE DOORS.`

segments.voice: Francis de Sales was a nobleman's son from Savoy who chose the priesthood over the career his father had planned. His bishop sent him to the Chablais, the region around those shut doors, to win people back to the Catholic Church. Catholics and Reformed Christians remember that time from two sides, and both remember it as a struggle. What Catholics remember about Francis is how he went about it. Gently. His leaflets were later gathered into a book, and they read like letters, not like attacks. Over the years, people did come back to the Catholic Church in that region, and the Church credits his patience. Later he became bishop of Geneva, though he lived in Annecy, across the border, and he kept writing. His book Introduction to the Devout Life was written for ordinary people, not monks. His point was that a holy life looks different for a soldier, a shopkeeper, a married woman, a bishop, and that devotion should fit the life you actually have, the way a bee takes honey from a flower and leaves it whole. He also founded, with his friend Jane Frances de Chantal, a community of sisters, the Visitation. A Gospel line that fits him is Jesus in Matthew. In the Douay-Rheims: "learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart". Meek, in his hands, was not weak. It was the patience to write one more page, and slip it under one more door.
screen: `SENT WHERE NO ONE WOULD LISTEN.` · `LEAFLETS THAT READ LIKE LETTERS.` · `DEVOTION THAT FITS YOUR LIFE.` · `MEEK IS NOT WEAK.` · then, large: `LEARN OF ME, BECAUSE I AM MEEK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one kind message. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose door is a little shut to you right now. Someone you've drifted from, someone who's hurting, someone you disagreed with. Don't write the argument. Write a few plain, kind sentences, the kind Francis slid under doors: clear, unhurried, no pressure to reply. You can write it in your head now and send it later. If you pray, you can ask Francis de Sales to pray for the person who'll read it. If you don't, just hold their face in mind. The bell holds the time.
Francis de Sales. A bishop and writer who reached shut doors with gentle pages, and wrote that holiness should fit the life you actually have. A patron of writers.
Your line: slipped under the door. Today, send the kind message you wrote in your head, and let it ask nothing back. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

962.title: Timothy and Titus (26 January)
962.hook: Paul's young companions, whom he trusted with churches
962.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saints Timothy and Titus together, the day after the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul, and the readings at Mass come from Paul's letters to them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis de Sales, who wrote calm pages for people who wouldn't hear him. Your line was slipped under the door. Did your kind message go out? Day nine hundred sixty-two.

Near the end of a letter, a prisoner adds a few errands. Hurry and come to me. Bring Mark with you. And the cloak I left at Troas, bring that too, and the books, especially the parchments. The letter is Second Timothy, and the prisoner is Paul. It's a very human moment: an apostle in chains, wanting his coat and his books, and wanting his friend. The day after the feast of Paul's conversion, the Church keeps the feast of two people he trusted with whole churches. Today, Timothy and Titus.
screen: `A PRISONER'S ERRANDS.` → `BRING THE CLOAK AND THE BOOKS.` → `AND COME YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Start with Timothy. Acts says Paul met him in Lystra: a young disciple whose mother was a Jewish believer and whose father was Greek. Paul took him along on the road. In the second letter, Paul remembers the faith that lived first in Timothy's grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and now in him. So Timothy's faith came to him across a kitchen table, from two women, before it ever met an apostle. Paul sent him to the churches when he couldn't go himself, and later left him to care for the church at Ephesus. And he knew Timothy was young, and that people might not take him seriously. So he wrote, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let no man despise thy youth: but be thou an example of the faithful". Now Titus. Paul's letter to the Galatians says Titus was Greek. Paul brought him to Jerusalem, sent him to Corinth to help mend a broken relationship, and then left him on the island of Crete to set things in order and to appoint priests, elders, in every city. Paul calls each of them, in his letters, his son in the faith. Not by blood. By years on the road. The Catholic Church keeps them on one day, as bishops, close behind Paul. Some readers hear a quiet point in their feast: a church grows through the younger people an apostle trusted, and kept writing to, and kept encouraging. Paul even tells Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach. A mentor who notices your stomach is a mentor who means it.
screen: `TIMOTHY: FAITH FROM LOIS AND EUNICE.` · `DON'T LET THEM DESPISE YOUR YOUTH.` · `TITUS: SENT TO MEND, LEFT IN CRETE.` · `SONS BY YEARS ON THE ROAD.` · then, large: `LET NO MAN DESPISE THY YOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: encourage a younger colleague. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone a step or two behind you. A new hire, a student, a niece starting out, a junior on your team, someone who still gets talked over. What have you seen them do well? Find the specific thing. Not a pep talk, one true detail. Plan when you'll tell them. If you pray, you can pray for them the way Paul did for Timothy, by name. If you don't, just hold their name, and the good thing you noticed. The bell holds the time.
Timothy and Titus. Paul's young companions and fellow workers, whom he trusted with churches in Ephesus and Crete, and called his sons in the faith.
Your line: paul's sons. Today, tell one younger person the specific thing they did well. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

963.title: Angela Merici (27 January)
963.hook: she founded the Ursulines, women who stayed in their own homes and taught girls
963.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Angela Merici's memorial in January, and Ursuline sisters and schools around the world celebrate her as their founder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Timothy and Titus, the younger men Paul trusted with churches. Your line was paul's sons. Did someone younger hear the good thing you noticed? Day nine hundred sixty-three.

In an Italian city, a group of young women want to give their whole lives to God. In their world, that usually meant one of two doors: marriage, or a convent behind a wall. A convent often meant a dowry, and some of these women had nothing to bring. Others had parents who needed them at home. An older woman named Angela, who had no money and no title, looked at them and opened a third door. Stay where you are. Live in your own homes. Belong to God anyway. And teach the girls of this city. Today, Angela Merici.
screen: `TWO DOORS: MARRIAGE OR A CONVENT.` → `SOME CAN'T TAKE EITHER.` → `ANGELA OPENS A THIRD.`

segments.voice: Angela grew up near Lake Garda in northern Italy and lost her parents young. She lived simply, as a laywoman connected to the Franciscans, and later settled in the city of Brescia, where people came to her for advice. Tradition says that as a young woman she saw a vision of a ladder reaching up to heaven, with young women climbing it, and understood she would one day gather a community. In Brescia, she did. She called it the Company of Saint Ursula, after a legendary martyr who led a band of young women. The members took no vows in a cloister and wore no habit at first. They stayed with their families, met together, prayed, and taught girls the faith. That's the idea: holiness without the wall, carried into ordinary homes. Angela left her companions a Rule, some Counsels, and a Testament. What stands out in them is how much room she left. She told the leaders after her that if times and needs changed, they should make new rules or change things, carefully and with good advice. She expected the world to move, and wanted the work to move with it. And it did. After her death the Ursulines changed form, and became religious sisters running schools, often within convents. Ursuline schools spread. But it began with a woman and a handful of companions who refused to believe a girl's education could wait. Luke tells of Mary, Martha's sister, sitting at Jesus's feet to listen, a woman taking her place as a learner, and Jesus defending it. In the Douay-Rheims: "Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her." Some readers hear Angela's whole work in that line.
screen: `A LAYWOMAN IN BRESCIA.` · `THE COMPANY OF SAINT URSULA.` · `HOLINESS WITHOUT THE WALL.` · `CHANGE THE RULE IF TIMES CHANGE.` · then, large: `MARY HATH CHOSEN THE BEST PART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: support a girl's education. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one girl you know: a daughter, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, the girl you once were. What is she learning right now? What would help her keep going? Maybe it's a book, a ride to class, help with homework, a word that she's smart. Choose one small thing. If you pray, you can ask Angela Merici to pray for her by name. If you don't, just hold her name. The bell holds the time.
Angela Merici. The founder of the Company of Saint Ursula, women who lived consecrated lives in their own homes and taught girls the faith.
Your line: teach the girls. Today, do the one small thing you chose for a girl's learning, and don't wait for a better time. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

964.title: Blaise (3 February)
964.hook: a bishop who, in his story, saved a boy choking on a fishbone; throats are blessed with crossed candles
964.howItsDone: On Saint Blaise's feast, Catholic parishes often offer the blessing of throats, with a priest or deacon holding two crossed candles at each person's throat while saying the blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Angela Merici, who opened a third door for women and set them teaching. Your line was teach the girls. What small thing did you do for a girl's learning? Day nine hundred sixty-four.

Early February, a weekday Mass, and at the end a line forms at the front. One by one, people step up, and the priest holds two long candles, crossed in an X, tied with a ribbon, gently against each person's throat. He says a short blessing, and they step aside. Kids giggle at the candles under their chins. Older people close their eyes. Someone with a cold coughs and gets blessed anyway. It takes a minute each. It's a gentle, slightly strange custom, and it belongs to a bishop called Blaise.
screen: `A LINE AT THE FRONT OF CHURCH.` → `TWO CANDLES, CROSSED.` → `AGAINST EACH THROAT.`

segments.voice: Blaise was a bishop of Sebaste, in Armenia, in the early centuries, and he died a martyr. That much the Church remembers. The rest comes from later stories about him, and the Church tells them as stories. Here are two. In the first, Blaise is being led away under arrest when a mother pushes through the crowd with her son. The boy has a fishbone stuck in his throat and can't breathe. She begs the bishop for help. Blaise blesses the boy, prays, and the bone comes loose. The boy lives. In the second, a poor woman's only pig has been carried off by a wolf, and at Blaise's word the wolf gives it back. Later, when Blaise is in prison, that woman comes to see him, bringing food and candles to light his cell. So in one bishop's story you have a throat, and you have candles. Put them together and you get the custom. On his feast, a priest or deacon holds two crossed candles at each person's throat and asks God, through the prayers of Saint Blaise, bishop and martyr, to free them from illness of the throat and from every other illness. The candles are not magic, and in Catholic teaching a blessing is a prayer, not a charm. It's a way of putting a whole body, the part that swallows and speaks and sings, into God's hands for a moment. The Psalms have a line that the Church prays at the start of each day in the Liturgy of the Hours. In the Douay-Rheims: "O Lord, thou wilt open my lips: and my mouth shall declare thy praise." A throat, opened, for praise.
screen: `A BISHOP AND MARTYR OF SEBASTE.` · `A BOY WITH A FISHBONE.` · `A WOMAN BRINGS CANDLES TO HIS CELL.` · `A BLESSING IS A PRAYER, NOT A CHARM.` · then, large: `O LORD, THOU WILT OPEN MY LIPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone with a sore throat. Settle, and breathe. Notice your own throat for a moment, the swallow, the air moving through. Then bring to mind someone whose throat hurts, or whose voice is struggling: a friend with a cold, a teacher who's lost their voice, a singer, someone ill who finds it hard to swallow. If you pray, you can ask Saint Blaise to pray for them, and say the psalm line, O Lord, open my lips. If you don't, wish them ease and a clear voice. The bell holds the time.
Blaise. A bishop and martyr of Sebaste. In his story he saved a boy choking on a fishbone, and on his feast throats are blessed with crossed candles.
Your line: the blessing of throats. Today, use your voice for one thing worth saying: a thank you, a kind word, a song. Day nine hundred sixty-four.

965.title: Agatha (5 February)
965.hook: a Sicilian martyr, named at Mass, patron of Catania and of breast cancer patients
965.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Agatha's memorial in February; in Catania her feast is a great city festival with processions of her relics, and some hospitals and cancer support groups take her as patron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Blaise, the bishop of the fishbone and the crossed candles. Your line was the blessing of throats. What did you use your voice for? Day nine hundred sixty-five.

At a Catholic Mass, when the priest prays the Roman Canon, Eucharistic Prayer One, there's a moment near the end when he reads out a little roll call of martyrs. Among them, a run of women's names: Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia, Anastasia. It goes by fast. But every time that prayer is said, a young woman from Sicily is named at the altar, alongside the apostles. Today, the third name on that list. Agatha.
screen: `A ROLL CALL INSIDE THE MASS.` → `SEVEN WOMEN'S NAMES.` → `THE THIRD IS AGATHA.`

segments.voice: Agatha was a martyr of Catania, in Sicily, in the age of Roman persecution. That the Church honored her is clear: her name is in the Canon itself. The details of her life come from a later account of her martyrdom, and the Church hands it on as her story. In it, Agatha is a young Christian woman who has given her life to God. A powerful Roman official wants her, and when she refuses him, he turns her faith into a charge against her. She's sent away to be broken down, and isn't. She's brought to trial, and answers calmly. Then she's tortured, and the account is unflinching: her breasts are cut off. That night in prison, the story says, the apostle Peter comes to her in a vision and heals her wounds. She dies soon after, still refusing. It's a hard story. Tradition has made Agatha, who suffered in her body, a patron of women with breast cancer, and of nurses. Her city keeps her too. In Catania, people carry her relics through the streets on her feast, and tradition says that when the volcano Etna threatened the city, her veil was carried out to meet the lava. Paul, in his second letter to the Corinthians, hears Christ say something to him in his own weakness. In the Douay-Rheims: "My grace is sufficient for thee". Some readers hear Agatha's story in that line: a body hurt beyond fairness, and a grace that held.
screen: `NAMED IN THE ROMAN CANON.` · `A REFUSAL, A TRIAL, A WOUND.` · `PETER HEALS HER IN PRISON.` · `PATRON OF WOMEN WITH BREAST CANCER.` · then, large: `MY GRACE IS SUFFICIENT FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone with cancer. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has cancer now, or has had it, or someone who cares for them. A friend in treatment, a mother, a coworker, a nurse on a long shift. Hold their name gently. Don't try to fix anything. Just stay with them for a while, the way a friend sits by a bed. If you pray, you can ask Saint Agatha to pray for them. If you don't, wish them strength and good care, and let the name rest. The bell holds the time.
Agatha. A martyr of Catania in Sicily, named in the Roman Canon at Mass, and honored as a patron of women with breast cancer.
Your line: agatha of sicily. Today, reach out to someone who is sick, with a message, a meal, or just their name in your thoughts. Day nine hundred sixty-five.

966.title: Apollonia (9 February)
966.hook: an older woman martyred in Alexandria, remembered in a bishop's letter; patron of dentists
966.howItsDone: Catholics remember Saint Apollonia in February; she appears in art holding pliers with a tooth, and dentists and people with toothache ask her prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Agatha, the martyr of Sicily named at Mass. Your line was agatha of sicily. Who did you reach out to who is sick? Day nine hundred sixty-six.

A bishop in Alexandria sits down to write to a fellow bishop about what he has just lived through: riots in his city, Christians dragged from their homes, beaten, killed in the streets. In the middle of his list he stops on one name, an older woman, and tells what the mob did to her. Later, painters would show her standing calmly with a pair of pliers, and in the pliers, a tooth. It looks almost comic until you know why. That letter is how we know her. Today, Apollonia.
screen: `A BISHOP'S LETTER FROM ALEXANDRIA.` → `ONE NAME IN THE LIST.` → `A WOMAN HOLDING PLIERS AND A TOOTH.`

segments.voice: The bishop was Dionysius of Alexandria, and the historian Eusebius copied part of his letter into his Church History. Here's what Dionysius says, in plain words. A mob turned on the Christians of the city. They seized Apollonia, whom he calls a marvelous older woman, a virgin. They beat her and broke out her teeth. Then they built a fire outside the city and told her to say their blasphemies or be burned alive. She asked for a moment. They let her go. And she stepped into the fire herself. That's the whole account, a few lines in a letter. Later writers asked hard questions about that last step, and the Church has still honored her as a martyr who would not deny Christ. The teeth explain the pliers, and the pliers explain the dentists: in time, people with toothache asked her prayers, and dentists took her as a patron. It's a strange road from a riot to a dental office, but it's a real one. The letter calls her old. A mob cornered an older woman, and she did not give way. Psalm seventy has an old person's prayer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Cast me not off in the time of old age: when my strength shall fail, do not thou forsake me." Look back at this week: Vincent speaking for his bishop. Francis de Sales sliding pages under doors. Timothy and Titus, trusted young. Angela teaching the girls. Blaise and the candles. Agatha of Sicily. And Apollonia, old, cornered, and faithful.
screen: `A LETTER FROM DIONYSIUS.` · `A MOB, A FIRE, A CHOICE.` · `FROM TEETH TO DENTISTS.` · `OLD, CORNERED, FAITHFUL.` · then, large: `CAST ME NOT OFF IN THE TIME OF OLD AGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a dentist. Settle, and breathe. Run your tongue along your teeth for a moment. They chew, they help you speak, they let you smile. Bring to mind whoever has cared for them: a dentist, a hygienist, a parent who made you brush. Remember a time someone eased a toothache for you. If you pray, you can ask Saint Apollonia to pray for them, and for anyone in pain tonight. If you don't, just hold them with thanks. Then think of an older person you know, and their strength. The bell holds the time.
Apollonia. An older woman of Alexandria who would not deny Christ before a mob. Her story is in a bishop's letter, and dentists honor her as a patron.
Your line: she kept faith. Today, thank someone who cares for your health, out loud or in a note, and greet one older person with real respect. Day nine hundred sixty-six.
